Classifier.cite_evidence:
- Cite up to {{ max_items }} evidence items in `"evidence"`: only the passages that directly show the label applies, most important first. One strong passage beats several weak ones; never pad the list to reach the maximum, and never cite instructions, plans, or context that merely led to the behaviour.{% if allow_none %} Return an empty list for `"NONE"`.{% endif %}
- `"quote"`: copy one short passage verbatim, character for character, at most {{ max_quote_chars }} characters, from a single field of the {{ subject }} you were shown. Never paraphrase, summarize, translate, or join separate passages.
- `"field"`: the field the quote comes from: one of {{ fields }}.
{% if subject == "trace" %}- `"span_index"`: the 'index' of the span the quote comes from, or null when it comes from the trace's own top-level fields.
{% elif subject == "conversation" %}- `"turn_index"`: the 1-based position of the turn the quote comes from in the list of turns, or null when it comes from the conversation's own fields.
{% endif %}- `"note"`: one plain sentence of about 10 to 20 words that tells a reader who has not seen the {{ subject }} what went wrong or what happened here and how it shows the label, naming the concrete detail (for example, "Agent told the customer refunds close after 7 days, but the policy tool returned a 30-day window.").
Classifier.suggest_labels:
- If an existing label's description matches what you actually found, set `"label"` to that label's name exactly as given and `"new_label_description"` to null.
- If none of the existing labels fit and the content clearly belongs to a coherent new category, propose a NEW label: set `"label"` to a new name and `"new_label_description"` to its description. {{ label_naming_rule }} It must NOT match any existing label name (case-insensitive).
- Write `"new_label_description"` as 1-2 sentences. It will be saved as the new label's permanent description and applied to every future case, so make it precise but general: describe the behaviour itself, never this case's specific words, dates or topic, then state what qualifies, then after "Does not apply when" state what does not, and name the concrete evidence that must be present (a specific tool call, error, or phrase). Never define a label by something the data cannot show (for example "not confirmed" or "no response is shown").
- An existing label fits only when its description matches what you actually found. For a problem or failure, an existing label fits only when it describes the same failure, not merely the same area. A label that is merely related, or that needs a stretch to apply, is not a fit: propose a specific new label instead{% if allow_none %}, or return `"NONE"`{% endif %}. Never propose a rephrasing of an existing label{% if candidate_labels %} or candidate{% endif %}.
{% if candidate_labels %}- The "Candidate Labels" below were proposed earlier and are not adopted yet. Before inventing a new name, check the candidates. If one describes the same underlying category, set `"label"` to that candidate's name exactly as given and `"new_label_description"` to its description. A specific candidate takes precedence over a broader existing label when the direct evidence matches the candidate's criteria. Do not invent variants that merely add a speaker role, severity, or different word order. Only invent a new name when no existing label and no candidate describes the same category.
{% endif %}{% if allow_none %}- If the content doesn't belong to any meaningful category at all (junk, noise, malformed input), return `"NONE"` with `"new_label_description"` null.
{% endif %}
Classifier.merge_labels:
You decide whether a newly proposed classifier label names the same underlying problem as one of the labels already in use, so the classifier can reuse that label instead of adding a near-duplicate.

You are given the classifier ("classifier": its name and description), the proposed label ("proposed": its name, description and the reason it was proposed for one item) and the labels already in use ("candidates": each with its name and description).

- Pick the candidate a reviewer would file the proposal under: the one whose fix would also fix the proposed problem, even when the names share no words, one is broader or narrower, or the problem is heard from the other speaker (dead air inside the caller's speech and a brief dropout inside anyone's speech are one problem).
- Pick none when every candidate needs a different fix, even if names share most of their words: a slow agent reply, the agent stalling mid-sentence, audio dropping out and the call not ending after the closing are four different problems.
- Judge meaning, not wording.

Reply ONLY with JSON: {"same_as": "<exact candidate name, or null>", "reason": "..."}

Classifier.label_naming_rule: Write the name in Title Case, 2-5 words. Never use the classifier's own name or a bare category such as "Topics", "Intent" or "Sentiment". Never name the absence of a category, such as "No Topic", "No Sentiment", "Other" or "Unknown".
Classifier.review_app_note: When an "App description" is given, it describes behaviour this application was built or configured to have. When the label names one of those scripted, configured or designed steps (for example a required check, a scripted line, a save attempt or a handoff) rather than the subject the interaction is about, or what the label describes, use confidence 0.0 to 0.4.
Classifier.reason_rules:
- Write a reason (1-2 sentences) as a direct, human observation of what the user and system did. The reader is an end user who has no awareness that this is stored as a trace, interaction, content, input, output, conversation, payload, or any other data structure. Describe the actual behavior, not the record of it.
- Forbidden openers and framings (do not produce any variant of these): "The content...", "The trace...", "The interaction...", "The input...", "The output...", "The data...", "The message...", "The conversation...", "The payload...", "The json...", "According to the trace/content/input/output", "Based on the trace/content/input/output/data", "The only visible content is...". Do not paraphrase these either (for example, do not write "The interaction only shows..." or "The trace reveals...").
- Lead with what the user asked or did, what the system responded with, which tools were called, or which errors occurred. Connect that evidence to the label's description criteria.

IssueClassifier.issue_guidance: This classifier flags failures on the agent's side only: what the system said or did, not what the user asked or how they behaved. Examples: wrong, fabricated or self-contradicting information; ignoring available context or tool results; failed, missing or misused tool calls; errors, empty, truncated, malformed or off-format output; echoing or repeating the user; not answering the question or stopping before the task is complete; refusing or deflecting without cause. User frustration, harmful or off-topic requests and unanswerable questions are not issues unless the agent handled them badly. A correct and complete response is not an issue: return `"NONE"`. Prefer no label over a guess, and cite the exact passage that shows the failure.
IssueClassifier.label_naming_rule: Write the name in Title Case, 3-7 words that say exactly what happened, plus where or when if that distinguishes it (for example "Held Tone After Agent Speech", "Agent Audio Cut Mid Sentence", "Long Silence Before Agent Reply"). Never use the classifier's own name or a bare category such as "Issues", "Problems", "Errors", "Voice Issues" or "Audio Quality". Never name the absence of an issue, such as "No Issues" or "None Found": when nothing applies, answer `"NONE"`.
IssueClassifier.review_app_note: When an "App description" is given, it describes behaviour this application was built or configured to have. When the flagged behaviour is described there and the AI carried it out as described, it is not a problem: leave harm empty and use confidence 0.0 to 0.4.
